subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the radical centre of the circles x² + y² + 4x − 7 = 0, 2x² + 2y² + 3x + 5y − 9 = 0, x² + y² + y = 0.

mark_split.label: Write the circles in standard form

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Sr. Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.54 — SAQ chapter 7 System of Circles, answer 53.2, on a ★★★ Super Scoring Page (SSP 54). Chapter star rank ★★★, per the SAQ section table (book p.49). Printed appearance tag: TS 16. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, same 1+1+1+1 reasoning as the twin answer 53.1 (this card's own verification note carries the full justification: patterned on Circle SAQ answer 48's four printed 1-mark tags, book p.51). This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. METHOD NOTE (not an error): the book scales every circle to a common leading coefficient of 2 before subtracting (writing S as 2x²+2y²+8x−14=0), which is a valid way to keep the leading coefficients matched; this card instead DIVIDES the middle circle by 2 to bring every circle to the standard x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0 form first, which is the more usual textbook method. Both routes give the identical radical axes and the identical radical centre (2, 1), checked independently. insider_note: The middle circle is printed with a leading coefficient of 2 — divide it by 2 before doing anything else. If it is subtracted as printed, the x² and y² terms do not cancel, and what is left is not a straight line at all, so it cannot be a radical axis.

steps.label: Write the circles in standard form
steps.margin_note: First mark. Every circle must show 1 as the coefficient of x² and y² before any radical axis is written.
lines: S − S′ needs x² and y² with coefficient 1

lines.text: in both, so divide this one by 2:

steps.why: The formula S − S′ = 0 for a radical axis only works when both circles already have coefficient 1 on x² and y² — dividing the middle circle by its leading coefficient 2 puts it in that form.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the circles before dividing the middle one by 2 — the x² and y² terms then do not cancel, so the result is not a straight line at all.
Dividing only the x² term by 2 and forgetting the y² term.
steps.memory_tip: Same coefficient on x² and y² in every circle, always 1, before the first subtraction — check this line before writing anything else.

steps.label: Find the two radical axes
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both axes come from the same fixed circle S, paired with S′ and then S″.
lines: Radical axis of S, S′ is S − S′ = 0
Radical axis of S, S″ is S − S″ = 0
steps.why: Subtracting the standard-form circles cancels x² and y², leaving one straight line per pair — two lines are enough to fix a single meeting point.
common_mistakes: Sign slip on the −9/2 constant term, which is easy to drop while clearing the fraction.
Mixing S′ into the second subtraction instead of S″.
steps.memory_tip: S stays fixed on the left in both subtractions — only the circle on the right changes.
lines_compact: Radical axis of S, S′ is S − S′ = 0
Radical axis of S, S″ is S − S″ = 0

steps.label: Solve the two axes
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for solving the pair correctly.

lines.text: Both have −y, so subtracting removes y:

steps.why: Solving equations (1) and (2) together gives the one point common to both radical axes — the radical centre.
common_mistakes: Subtracting in the order (1) − (2) and then losing a sign: it gives −3x + 6 = 0, which still means x = 2.
Using S′ instead of S − S′'s own equation (1) when finding y.
steps.memory_tip: Look for a variable whose coefficients already match — here y, with −1 in both — and subtract to remove it; no scaling was needed this time.

steps.label: State the radical centre
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark, for the final coordinate pair.
steps.why: The point (2, 1) has equal power with respect to all three circles — every pairwise radical axis passes through it.
common_mistakes: Writing the pair as (1, 2) instead of (2, 1).
Forgetting to check that the point also satisfies the third circle's implicit radical axis (S′ − S″), which it always will once (1) and (2) both hold.
steps.memory_tip: A clean integer pair like (2, 1) is a good sign the two radical axes were solved correctly — a messy fraction is worth double-checking.
